# Unit 1: Physics and Human Society
## 1.1 Definition and Nature of Physics
*Grade 9 Physics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 1 of 173 (PDF Page 7) • Grade 9 Physics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (1.1 Definition and Nature of Physics):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 2):** Meaning of physics as the fundamental study of matter, energy, space, time, and their interactions.
> • Curriculum Focus: Meaning of physics as the fundamental study of matter, energy, space, time, and their interactions.
> • Meaning & Scope of Physics: Physics (from the Greek word "phusis" meaning nature) is the fundamental natural science that investigates matter, energy, space, time, and their reciprocal interactions. Its scope ranges from subatomic quarks (10⁻¹⁸ m) to the cosmic expanse (10²⁶ m).
> • Core Branches of Physics (Table 1.1 in Textbook): 1) Mechanics (motion with or without reference to forces); 2) Thermodynamics (heat, temperature, and energy transformations); 3) Optics (light properties, lenses, and lasers); 4) Electromagnetism (electric charges, currents, and magnetic fields); 5) Acoustics (sound production and wave transmission); 6) Nuclear & Quantum Physics (atomic nuclei, radioactivity, and energy quantization).
> • Interdisciplinary Fields: Biophysics (applying physics laws to biological mechanisms and nerve impulses); Geophysics (seismic waves and tectonic activity in the Ethiopian Rift Valley); Medical Physics (X-rays, ultrasound, MRI, radiotherapy); Astrophysics (celestial dynamics and cosmology).
> • Historical Contributors in the Ethiopian Curriculum: Galileo Galilei (scientific method & kinematics); Sir Isaac Newton (laws of motion and universal gravitation); Michael Faraday (electromagnetic induction); Marie Curie (radioactivity discoveries); Albert Einstein (theory of relativity & photoelectric effect).
> • Physics in Ethiopian National Modernization: Hydroelectric generation at the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD, 5,150 MW), satellite communication via ET-SMART, and regional medical imaging infrastructure.

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 1 — Structured Curriculum Text

Unit 1

Physics and Human Society

Introduction

Brainstorming

Questions

T Explain science

and its broad categories.

T What are the

main branches of

natural science?

You learnt about general science in lower grades. General science includes subjects like Biology, Chemistry and Physics. Therefore, in this grade level and in

higher grades, you will learn about each of the three subjects and explore their

beauty. In this unit you will learn about physics and the human society. In particular, you will learn about definition of physics, different branches of physics,

relationship between physics and other fields of study, contributions of prominent scientists in advancing physics, and the way physics knowledge was evolving

and changing in history.

At the end of this unit, you should be able to:

• define physics in different ways;

• describe the different branches of physics;

• describe the relationships between physics and other fields of study;

• discuss the contributions of prominent scientists in advancing physics at

different periods of time;

• describe how aspects of physics are used in other sciences (e. g. biology,

chemistry, engineering, etc.) as well as in everyday technology; and

• discuss how physics knowledge was evolving and changing in history.

---

### 📖 Structured AI Concept Breakdown & Explanation

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Physics investigates the governing principles of the universe. From subatomic particles to cosmic galaxy clusters, physical laws quantify cause-and-effect relationships and drive modern technological infrastructure.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Meaning of physics as the fundamental study of matter, energy, space, time, and their interactions.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Physics forms the empirical and theoretical foundation for all engineering disciplines and modern technology.
- **Key Principle**: The classical branches are Mechanics, Thermodynamics, Optics, Acoustics, and Electromagnetism; modern branches include Quantum Mechanics and Relativity.
- **Key Principle**: GERD converts gravitational potential energy (mgh) of the Blue Nile into kinetic energy of rotating turbines, generating electrical induction.

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Branches of Physics (Table 1.1): [Classical: Mechanics, Thermodynamics, Optics, Acoustics, Electromagnetism] ◄──► [Modern: Relativity, Quantum Physics, Nuclear Physics]. Contributors: Galileo ──> Newton ──> Faraday ──> Curie ──> Einstein.
```


| Parameter / Aspect | Academic Specification & Meaning | National Syllabus Standard |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Core Topic** | 1.1 Definition and Nature of Physics | Unit 1 Framework |
| **Governing Law** | Physics studies matter, energy, and their fundamental interactions; classical br... | Formulated per MoE Guidelines |
| **Examination Traps** | Frequent in EUEE: identifying branches of physics, distinguishing classical vs m... | Critical EUEE Target Point |

### 4. Real-World Ethiopian Application & Technological Context
The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Abay River, Ethiopian Space Science and Technology Institute (ESSTI), and Aluto-Langano geothermal expansion demonstrate applied physics transforming Ethiopia.

### 5. EUEE Entrance Examination Strategy & Examiner Distractors
Frequent in EUEE: identifying branches of physics, distinguishing classical vs modern branches, energy conversion sequences in hydroelectric power stations, and applications of wave physics in medical diagnostics.

### 6. Comprehensive Student Takeaway
Physics studies matter, energy, and their fundamental interactions; classical branches govern macroscopic systems while modern physics governs relativistic and quantum phenomena.

> 💡 **Core Definition & Governing Principle:**
> **Definition and Nature of Physics:** Physics studies matter, energy, and their fundamental interactions; classical branches govern macroscopic systems while modern physics governs relativistic and quantum phenomena.

---

> 🇪🇹 **Ethiopian Real-World Application & Relevance:**
> The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Abay River, Ethiopian Space Science and Technology Institute (ESSTI), and Aluto-Langano geothermal expansion demonstrate applied physics transforming Ethiopia.

> ⚡ **EUEE National Exam Strategy & Common Trap:**
> Frequent in EUEE: identifying branches of physics, distinguishing classical vs modern branches, energy conversion sequences in hydroelectric power stations, and applications of wave physics in medical diagnostics.

---

### 🧮 Worked Step-by-Step Curriculum Example
**Problem:** Apply the governing principles of **Definition and Nature of Physics** to analyze and solve a standard Grade 9 Physics curriculum problem.

**Step-by-Step Solution:**
1. Physics forms the empirical and theoretical foundation for all engineering disciplines and modern technology.
2. The classical branches are Mechanics, Thermodynamics, Optics, Acoustics, and Electromagnetism; modern branches include Quantum Mechanics and Relativity.
3. GERD converts gravitational potential energy (mgh) of the Blue Nile into kinetic energy of rotating turbines, generating electrical induction.

---

### ✍️ Self-Check EUEE Review Question
**1. Which of the following statements regarding Definition and Nature of Physics is strictly valid according to the Ethiopian National Curriculum?**
- **A)** Physics studies matter, energy, and their fundamental interactions; classical branches govern macroscopic systems while modern physics governs relativistic and quantum phenomena.
- **B)** It operates independently of physical or theoretical boundary conditions.
- **C)** It yields arbitrary results regardless of initial system parameters.
- **D)** None of the above.

> ✅ **Correct Answer:** **A** — *Physics studies matter, energy, and their fundamental interactions; classical branches govern macroscopic systems while modern physics governs relativistic and quantum phenomena.*

The layout maps out a systematic pathway starting from brainstorming general science categories (Biology, Chemistry, Physics) to defining core unit outcomes such as defining physics, listing its branches, and analyzing historical scientific contributions.
ai_analysis.ethiopian_context: In the Ethiopian educational framework, Grade 9 physics builds upon regional primary school general science. Understanding these fundamental natural sciences serves as the critical intellectual foundation for future national engineering and infrastructural projects in Ethiopia, such as hydroelectric power generation at the GERD, telecommunications via satellite engineering, and regional medical imaging infrastructure.
ai_analysis.euee_insight: A common EUEE conceptual trap is confusing the broader scope of 'general science' from lower grades with the specific foundational domain of 'physics' as defined in secondary curriculum. ### 2.1 Scales, Standards, Units (prefixes)

Scales

Ay the end of this section, you should be able to:

• list the four type of scales;

• distinguish between the four types of scales.

In general there are four data measuring scales. These are nominal scales,

ordinal scales, interval scales and ratio scales.

### ✍️ Exercise 2.1

List different examples of ordinal

scales.

• Nominal scales: are used for labeling variables without any number value.

For nominal scales there is no inherent quantitative difference among the

categories. Examples are: gender (male, female), hair color (black, brown).

### ✍️ Exercise 2.2

List different examples of interval

scales.

• Ordinal scales: are rank-order observations. For this type of scale, there is

an underlying quantitative measurement on which the observations differ.

Example: Your class rank in the previous grades.

> **Key Concept:**

T In physics scale

is a set of numbers,

amounts, etc., used

to measure or compare the level of

something.

T Ratio scale is

an advanced scale

in which addition,

subtraction, multiplication and division is

possible.

• Interval scales: have a constant interval but lack a true zero point. For this

type of scale, one can add and subtract values on an interval scale, but one

cannot multiply or divide units. Temperature in Celsius or Fahrenheit scale

is an example of interval scale.

• Ratio scales: have the property of equal intervals but also have a true zero

point. As a result, one can multiply and divide as well as add and subtract

using ratio scales. Units of time (second, minute, hour), length (centimeter,

> • Fundamental vs Derived Physical Quantities: Fundamental base quantities are independent physical dimensions: Length (m), Mass (kg), Time (s), Electric Current (A), Temperature (K), Amount of Substance (mol), Luminous Intensity (cd). Derived quantities are defined algebraically from base quantities: Density (kg/m³), Force (N = kg·m/s²), Pressure (Pa = N/m²).

> • Errors in Measurement: Random Errors (unpredictable environmental fluctuations, minimized by taking repeated trials and calculating mean); Systematic Errors (zero error in instruments, faulty calibration, shift all measurements consistently in one direction).

# Unit 2: Physical Quantities
## 2.4 Unit Conversion
*Grade 9 Physics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 31 of 173 (PDF Page 37) • Grade 9 Physics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (2.4 Unit Conversion):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 26):** Conversion factors between metric and non-metric units for length, area, volume, mass, time, and speed.
> • Curriculum Focus: Conversion factors between metric and non-metric units for length, area, volume, mass, time, and speed.
> • Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
> • Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
> • Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
> • Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
> • Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
> • Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.

> • Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
> • Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
> • Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
> • Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
> • Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.

daily life.

In this unit, you will be introduced to the basic concepts of motion. We encounter

motion in our day-to-day activities and have enough experience about it. You

might have learnt in lower grades that everything in the universe moves. It is

because of this that motion is one of the key topics in physics. We use the basic

concepts of distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration to express

motion. There are different types of motions. Motion in a straight line is one of

the simplest forms of motion in a specific direction. The motions of a car on a

road, the motion of a train along a straight railway track or an object falling freely

are examples of one-dimensional motion.

• describe motion in terms of frame of reference, displacement, speed, velocity, and acceleration;

acceleration;

average velocity and acceleration.

school, your journey begins from your home. Your home is your original position.

After some time, you will reach your school. Your school is your final position.

In this process, you are continuously changing your position. While traveling

from home to school, you are increasing the gap between your present position

and your home. This continuous change of position is known as motion. Note

school to home. Your home is taken as a reference frame. Motion is a continuous

change in position of an object relative to the position of a fixed object called

reference frame.

T A frame of reference is a set of coordinates that can be used to determine positions of objects.

point as the time passes.

reference frame does not change with time. If the position of a body changes

with time in a frame of reference, the body is said to be in motion in that frame of

reference. The concepts of rest and motion are completely relative; a body at rest

in one reference frame may be in motion with respect to another reference frame.

For example, if you are 2 m from the doorway inside your classroom, then your

reference point is the doorway. Your classroom can be used as a reference frame.

In the classroom, the walls are not moving, and can be used as a fixed frame of

reference. We commonly use the origin as a fixed reference point to describe

motion along a straight line.

*Grade 9 Physics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 59 of 173 (PDF Page 65) • Grade 9 Physics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (4.1 The Concept of Force):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 60):** Vector nature of force, contact vs non-contact forces, gravitational weight W = mg, and net resultant force.
> • Curriculum Focus: Vector nature of force, contact vs non-contact forces, gravitational weight W = mg, and net resultant force.
> • Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.
> • Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.
> • Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).
> • Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.
> • Power & Mechanical Efficiency: Power P = Work / time = W / t = F · v (Watts W = J/s). Efficiency η = (Useful Work Output / Total Energy Input) × 100%.

the motion to occur. Treating motion in this way falls within the branch of mechanics called dynamics. In simple terms, a force can be thought of as simply a

push or a pull, but forces exist in a wide variety of situations in our daily lives and

### 4.1 The Concept of Force

At the end of this section, you should be able to:

• define force, and give examples of forces;

• practically measure the gravitational force on an object.

From your everyday experience, you have basic understanding of the concept

of force. Any time the state of motion of an object changes, a force has been

applied. Force can cause a stationary object to start moving or a moving object

to accelerate. You exert force to stretch or compress a spring, to throw or kick a

ball, to pick your books from a table, to fetch water from a river or well etc. In

mechanics, a force is a push or a pull exerted on a body that changes the state of

motion of the body. That means force can change the velocity of a body or cause

*Grade 9 Physics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 67 of 173 (PDF Page 73) • Grade 9 Physics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

> • Curriculum Focus: Newton's First Law (inertia), Second Law (F_net = ma), and Third Law (action and reaction).
> • Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.
> • Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.

When an object is in motion on a given rough surface, there is resistance to the

motion of the object from the surface. Such resistance is called force of friction

and is denoted by 'f'. Forces of friction are very important in our everyday lives.

They allow us to walk or run and are necessary for the motion of wheeled vehicles.

the force is applied in the same

direction as the direction of displacement of the box.

The word work has a variety of meanings in everyday language. In everyday

sense, the term work means to do something that takes physical or mental effort.

But in physics, work has a distinctly different meaning. Consider the following

situations:

• A student holds up a heavy chair for several minutes.

• A student carries a bucket of water along a horizontal path while walking at

a constant velocity.

It might surprise you to know that as the term work is used in physics, there is no

work done on the chair or the bucket, even though effort is required in both cases.

In physics, work means the use of force to move an object. Not all force that is

used to move an object does work. For work to be done, the force must be applied

78 Unit 4 Force, Work, Energy and Power

### 📝 Unit Summary

• A simple machine (Compound machine) is a device that makes

easier to do mechanical work.

• In mechanics, a force is a push or a pull exerted on a body that

changes the state of motion of the body. That means force can

change the velocity of a body or cause deformation by changing its

shape or size.

• Forces can be classified as contact and non-contact forces. Contact

forces involve physical contact between two bodies and the noncontact forces do not involve any physical contact

• Newton's first law of motion, sometimes called the law of inertia,

states that a body continues to be in its state of rest or of uniform

motion in a straight line unless it is acted on by unbalanced force.

• An inertial frame is defined as one in which Newton's first law of motion is valid. Any reference frame that moves with constant velocity

relative to an inertial frame is itself an inertial frame.

• Newton's second law of motion states that the acceleration of a

body is directly proportional to the force acting on it and inversely

proportional to the mass of the body.

• Action and reaction forces are equal in magnitude but opposite in

direction. Work is the product of a force and displacement parallel

to the direction of the force applied, or a transfer of energy from one

object to another through the force.

• Kinetic energy (Ek ) is the form of mechanical energy possessed by

an object due to its motion.

• Potential energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its

position or configuration.

• Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energies.

• Power is the rate at which the work is done or the rate at which

energy is being transferred.

> • Curriculum Focus: Definition of simple machines, force multipliers, speed/distance multipliers, and direction changers.
> • Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
> • Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
> • Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
> • Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
> • Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.

In this unit, you are going to study important concepts of simple machines. You

use knives to cut and chop different items and use pulley to lift water from a well.

An axe, knife and pulley are simple machines that help people to do work more

easily. Humans have been making and using simple machines for a long time.

We create these machines to help us to survive and do our work. We use these

machines every day and in all aspects of our lives. In this unit, students will learn

different types of simple machines, purpose of simple machines and mechanical

advantages of simple machines.

At the end of this unit, you should be able to:

• know the types of simple machines;

• define mechanical advantage and efficiency of a machine;

• solve problems related to simple machines;

• construct simple machines that are applicable to solve real problems in

their local area.

## 5.3 Simple Machines at Work Place
*Grade 9 Physics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 87 of 173 (PDF Page 93) • Grade 9 Physics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.3 Simple Machines at Work Place):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 87):** Construction, agricultural, and workshop machines: wheelbarrows, pulleys, jacks, ramps, axes, and wedges.
> • Curriculum Focus: Construction, agricultural, and workshop machines: wheelbarrows, pulleys, jacks, ramps, axes, and wedges.
> • Principles of Simple Machines: A simple machine transforms the magnitude or direction of an applied effort force to overcome a load. Mechanical Advantage MA = Load / Effort = L / E. Velocity Ratio VR = Effort Distance / Load Distance = d_E / d_L. Efficiency η = (MA / VR) × 100% = (Work Output / Work Input) × 100%.
> • Levers & Principle of Moments: Rigid bar pivoting on a fulcrum. Load × Load Arm = Effort × Effort Distance (L · d_L = E · d_E). Class 1 (Fulcrum in middle: crowbar, scissors); Class 2 (Load in middle, MA > 1: wheelbarrow, nutcracker); Class 3 (Effort in middle, MA < 1: tweezers, human forearm).
> • Pulley Systems: Single Fixed Pulley (VR = 1, changes force direction); Single Movable Pulley (VR = 2); Block and Tackle System (VR = n, number of supporting rope segments).
> • Inclined Plane, Wedge, Screw, Wheel & Axle: Inclined Plane VR = Length of incline / Height = L / h. Wedge (two inclined planes back-to-back). Screw (inclined plane wrapped around cylinder). Wheel & Axle VR = Radius of Wheel / Radius of Axle = R / r.

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 87 — Structured Curriculum Text

### 5.3 Simple Machines at Work Place 87

### 📋 Activity 5.3

Does a machine multiply a force and distance at the same time? Discuss

in groups.

> **Key Concept:**

T Simple (compound) machines are said to be force multipliers when

they enable us to lift big load by applying small effort. Load is greater than

effort.

T Simple (compound) machines are said to be distance multipliers when

they enable people to lift a load through a large distance by moving the

effort through a small distance.

### 5.3 Simple Machines at Work Place

At the end of this section, you should be able to:

• categorize simple machines at home and workplace according to their

type.

The development of the technology that created cars, airplanes, and other

modern conveniences began with the invention of simple machines. A simple

machine is a mechanical device that accomplishes a task with only one movement

(such as a lever). A lever allows you to move a rock that weighs 10 times (or more)

than your weight.

---

### 📖 Structured AI Concept Breakdown & Explanation

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Simple machines provide mechanical leverage. By extending the effort displacement distance, the required effort force is proportionately reduced, allowing heavy loads to be lifted easily.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Construction, agricultural, and workshop machines: wheelbarrows, pulleys, jacks, ramps, axes, and wedges.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Ideal machines have 100% efficiency (MA = VR); real machines always have efficiency η < 100% (MA < VR) due to internal friction.
- **Key Principle**: VR depends STRICTLY on the geometric dimensions of the machine and remains constant regardless of friction or load.
- **Key Principle**: In a block and tackle pulley system, VR equals the number of rope segments directly supporting the movable load.

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Machine Efficiency Triangle: VR (Geometric Ratio, fixed) ──(Friction Losses)──> MA (Real Force Ratio, MA < VR) ──> Efficiency η = (MA/VR) × 100%.
```

Hand-operated water pumps, traditional grain mills, and construction site block-and-tackle rigs across rural Ethiopia apply simple machine mechanical advantage.

Universal EUEE question: calculating efficiency given load, effort, and VR, identifying lever classes, calculating inclined plane VR = L/h, and counting block & tackle supporting ropes.

### 6. Comprehensive Student Takeaway
MA = Load/Effort; VR = d_effort/d_load; Efficiency η = (MA/VR) × 100%; VR depends solely on machine geometry.

## 5.5 Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency
*Grade 9 Physics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 92 of 173 (PDF Page 98) • Grade 9 Physics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.5 Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 92):** Actual MA (Load/Effort), Velocity Ratio VR (d_E/d_L), and Efficiency η = (MA/VR) × 100% calculations for all simple machines.
> • Curriculum Focus: Actual MA (Load/Effort), Velocity Ratio VR (d_E/d_L), and Efficiency η = (MA/VR) × 100% calculations for all simple machines.
> • Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
> • Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
> • Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
> • Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
> • Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
> • Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.

> • Curriculum Focus: Actual MA (Load/Effort), Velocity Ratio VR (d_E/d_L), and Efficiency η = (MA/VR) × 100% calculations for all simple machines.
> • Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
> • Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
> • Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
> • Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
> • Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
> • Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.

## 5.5 Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency
*Grade 9 Physics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 105 of 173 (PDF Page 111) • Grade 9 Physics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.5 Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 92):** Actual MA (Load/Effort), Velocity Ratio VR (d_E/d_L), and Efficiency η = (MA/VR) × 100% calculations for all simple machines.
> • Curriculum Focus: Actual MA (Load/Effort), Velocity Ratio VR (d_E/d_L), and Efficiency η = (MA/VR) × 100% calculations for all simple machines.
> • Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
> • Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
> • Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
> • Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
> • Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
> • Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 105 — Structured Curriculum Text

### 5.5 Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency of Simple Machine 105

> 🖼️ **Figure 5.19 Arrangement of wheel and axle (input force is used to turn the wheel).**

> *(Original textbook diagram/illustration — View crisp illustration in the "Exact Page" tab)*

• A lever is able to rotate through a complete circle (360 degree).

• The circle turned by the wheel is much larger than the circle turned by the

axle.

• The increased distance over which the force is applied as the wheel turns

results in a more powerful force on the axle, which moves a shorter distance.

• The larger the diameter of the wheel, the less effort you need to turn it, but

you have to move the wheel a greater distance to get the same work done.

There are two basic types of wheel and axle in simple machines.

1. A machine where the force is applied to the axle. Applying a large force to

the axle makes the wheel go faster. The mechanical advantage is less than

one and the output force is less than the input force. Everyday examples of

this type of wheel and axle include:

• Bicycle

• Car tires

• Electric fan

2. A machine where the force is applied to the wheel. When you apply a small

force to the wheel, it travels a longer distance and creates a stronger force on

---

### 📖 Structured AI Concept Breakdown & Explanation

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
1D Kinematics describes motion along a straight line without referencing the forces causing it. Mathematical equations and motion graph slopes connect position, velocity, acceleration, and time.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Actual MA (Load/Effort), Velocity Ratio VR (d_E/d_L), and Efficiency η = (MA/VR) × 100% calculations for all simple machines.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Displacement can be positive, negative, or zero, even when total distance traveled is large.
- **Key Principle**: The slope of a velocity-time (v-t) graph is acceleration; the area underneath the curve is displacement.
- **Key Principle**: Objects in free fall experience constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance).

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Motion Graph Rules: [s-t Graph Slope = Velocity v] ──> [v-t Graph Slope = Acceleration a] ──> [Area under v-t Graph = Displacement s].
```


| Parameter / Aspect | Academic Specification & Meaning | National Syllabus Standard |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Core Topic** | 5.5 Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency | Unit 5 Framework |
| **Governing Law** | Uniform 1D motion is governed by four kinematics equations; slope of v-t graph g... | Formulated per MoE Guidelines |
| **Examination Traps** | Very high frequency in EUEE: solving free fall problems (v = 0 at top), extracti... | Critical EUEE Target Point |

### 4. Real-World Ethiopian Application & Technological Context
Highway speed management and braking distance safety standards along the Addis-Adama Expressway are modeled using 1D kinematics equations.

### 5. EUEE Entrance Examination Strategy & Examiner Distractors
Very high frequency in EUEE: solving free fall problems (v = 0 at top), extracting acceleration and displacement from v-t graphs, and applying v² = u² + 2as.

### 6. Comprehensive Student Takeaway
Uniform 1D motion is governed by four kinematics equations; slope of v-t graph gives acceleration, and area under v-t graph gives displacement.

> 💡 **Core Definition & Governing Principle:**
> **Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency:** Uniform 1D motion is governed by four kinematics equations; slope of v-t graph gives acceleration, and area under v-t graph gives displacement.

---

> 🇪🇹 **Ethiopian Real-World Application & Relevance:**
> Highway speed management and braking distance safety standards along the Addis-Adama Expressway are modeled using 1D kinematics equations.

> ⚡ **EUEE National Exam Strategy & Common Trap:**
> Very high frequency in EUEE: solving free fall problems (v = 0 at top), extracting acceleration and displacement from v-t graphs, and applying v² = u² + 2as.

---

### 🧮 Worked Step-by-Step Curriculum Example
**Problem:** Apply the governing principles of **Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency** to analyze and solve a standard Grade 9 Physics curriculum problem.

**Step-by-Step Solution:**
1. Displacement can be positive, negative, or zero, even when total distance traveled is large.
2. The slope of a velocity-time (v-t) graph is acceleration; the area underneath the curve is displacement.
3. Objects in free fall experience constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance).

---

### ✍️ Self-Check EUEE Review Question
**1. Which of the following statements regarding Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency is strictly valid according to the Ethiopian National Curriculum?**
- **A)** Uniform 1D motion is governed by four kinematics equations; slope of v-t graph gives acceleration, and area under v-t graph gives displacement.
- **B)** It operates independently of physical or theoretical boundary conditions.
- **C)** It yields arbitrary results regardless of initial system parameters.
- **D)** None of the above.

> ✅ **Correct Answer:** **A** — *Uniform 1D motion is governed by four kinematics equations; slope of v-t graph gives acceleration, and area under v-t graph gives displacement.*

108 Unit 5 Simple Machines

Definition

A pulley is a circular body (wheel) with groove surface and is free to rotate

about its center.

A fixed pulley: comprises a fixed axle with the rope looped over the top. A

fixed pulley is used to change the direction of the force. A fixed pulley is the only

pulley that when used individually, uses more effort than the load to lift the load

from the ground. The fixed pulley when attached to an unmovable object e. g.

a ceiling or wall, acts as a first class lever with the fulcrum being located at the

axis but with a minor change, the bar becomes a rope. The advantage of the

fixed pulley is that you do not have to pull or push the pulley up and down. The

disadvantage is that you have to apply more effort than the load.

b) V. R = 4

c) V. R = 5

d) V. R = 6

A movable pulley: In this type of pulley the axle is free to move up and down.

For a movable pulley if one end of the rope is fixed, applying an effort to the other

end of the rope will effectively provide about 2 times a force. A movable pulley

has a V. R = 2 . That is in order to lift the load 1m you would have to pull 2 m of the

rope through the pulley. The main disadvantage of a movable pulley is that you

have to pull or push the pulley up or down. The main advantage of a movable

pulley is that you use less effort to pull the load.

For both a fixed and a movable pulley there are energy losses due to friction.

As the result mechanical advantage (M. A) is always less than the velocity ratio

(V. R).

A compound pulley: is the combination of a fixed and a movable pulley. This

is sometimes called a block and tackle. A combined pulley makes life easier as

the effort needed to lift the load is less than half the weight of the load. The

main advantage of this pulley is that the amount of effort is less than half of the

load. The main disadvantage is it travels a very long distance. Figure 5.21 shows

different pulley types.

# Unit 6: Mechanical Oscillation and Sound Wave
## 6.1 Common Characteristics of Waves
*Grade 9 Physics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 113 of 173 (PDF Page 119) • Grade 9 Physics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (6.1 Common Characteristics of Waves):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 114):** Amplitude, wavelength (λ), period (T), frequency (f = 1/T), wave speed (v = fλ), crests, troughs, compressions, and rarefactions.
> • Curriculum Focus: Amplitude, wavelength (λ), period (T), frequency (f = 1/T), wave speed (v = fλ), crests, troughs, compressions, and rarefactions.
> • Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
> • Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
> • Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
> • Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
> • Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.
> • Motion Graphs: Position-Time (s-t) slope = velocity; Velocity-Time (v-t) slope = acceleration; Area under v-t graph = displacement Δx.

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 113 — Structured Curriculum Text

Unit 6

Mechanical Oscillation and Sound

Wave

Brainstorming

Questions

Have you ever

played a swing,

guitar or kirar? Have

you ever slapped water with your hands

and observed what

happened? Discuss

such phenomena or

motion.

Introduction

Many systems oscillate, that is they move back and forth about a fixed point.

All oscillations involve force and energy. For example, you push a child in a

swing to get the motion started. You put energy into a guitar string when you

pluck it. Some oscillations create waves. A wave is a disturbance that moves

from its source accompanied by transfer of energy. A guitar creates sound

waves and you can make water waves in a swimming pool by slapping the

water with your hand. Some, such as water waves, are visible. Some, such as

sound waves, are not. Oscillation is also known as periodic motion. Periodic

motion is a motion that repeats itself. A small object oscillating at the end of

a spring, a swinging pendulum etc. are examples of periodic motion.

---

1D Kinematics describes motion along a straight line without referencing the forces causing it. Mathematical equations and motion graph slopes connect position, velocity, acceleration, and time.

- **Key Principle**: The slope of a velocity-time (v-t) graph is acceleration; the area underneath the curve is displacement.
- **Key Principle**: Objects in free fall experience constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass (ignoring air resistance).

> • Curriculum Focus: Amplitude, wavelength (λ), period (T), frequency (f = 1/T), wave speed (v = fλ), crests, troughs, compressions, and rarefactions.
> • Distance vs Displacement: Distance is total scalar path length (d ≥ 0). Displacement Δx is the shortest vector straight line from initial position x_i to final position x_f (Δx = x_f - x_i).
> • Speed vs Velocity: Speed = Total Distance / Time (scalar). Velocity v = Displacement / Time = Δx / Δt (vector). Instantaneous velocity v = lim_{Δt→0} (Δx / Δt).
> • Acceleration in 1D: Rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t (units: m/s²). Uniform acceleration means equal velocity changes in equal time intervals.
> • Equations of Uniformly Accelerated 1D Motion: 1) v = u + at; 2) s = ut + 0.5at²; 3) v² = u² + 2as; 4) s = [(u + v) / 2]t.
> • Vertical Free Fall Under Gravity: Motion under constant gravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (downward). At maximum height of a upward toss, instantaneous velocity v = 0 m/s.

> • Curriculum Focus: Transverse vs longitudinal waves, mechanical vs electromagnetic waves, and energy transfer without net matter transport.
> • Magnetic Lorentz Force: On a moving charge: F = q(v × B) = qvB sin θ. Direction given by Right-Hand Rule (RHR). Because force is perpendicular to velocity, magnetic fields do NO work on charges (speed and kinetic energy remain constant; path curves into circle of radius r = mv / (qB)).
> • Force on Current-Carrying Wire: F = I(L × B) = ILB sin θ. Parallel currents attract; anti-parallel currents repel.
> • Sources of Magnetic Field: Magnetic field of long straight wire: B = (μ_0·I) / (2πr). Field inside solenoid: B = μ_0·n·I (n = N/L). Ampère's Law: ∮ B·dl = μ_0·I_enc.
> • Faraday's Law & Lenz's Law: Magnetic flux Φ_B = B·A cos θ. Induced EMF: ε = -N(dΦ_B / dt). Lenz's Law (Energy Conservation): Induced current creates a magnetic field that OPPOSES the original change in flux.
> • Transformers: Operates strictly on alternating current via mutual induction: V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p = I_p / I_s. Step-up transformer increases voltage while decreasing current to minimize transmission I²R line losses.

### 📄 Textbook Page 123 — Structured Curriculum Text

### 6.3 Propagation of Waves and Energy Transmission 123

### 6.3 Propagation of Waves and Energy Transmission

At the end of this section, you should be able to:

• differentiate between mechanical, electromagnetic, longitudinal, and

transverse waves;

• give examples of mechanical, electromagnetic, longitudinal, and transverse waves;

• describe the propagation of waves practically using string and water.

A wave is an oscillation that travels from one place to another. A musician's

instrument creates waves that carry sound to your ears. Dialing a cell phone to

call a friend sends microwaves from the cell phone antenna; the microwaves carry

the signal containing your voice to your friend. Similarly, when you throw a stone

into a pond, the energy of the falling stone creates waves in the water that carry

the energy to the edge of the pond. Do you think waves require material medium

for their propagation? In this section we see that some waves need material

medium for their propagation, while others do not need material medium. Waves

that require material medium for their propagation are called Mechanical waves.

Other types of waves known as electromagnetic waves do not need material

medium for their propagation.

Mechanical waves travel through a material as a vibration of the particles of

the material (water, wood, air, etc.). It is these vibrations that form the wave. All

mechanical waves require a medium to travel through. Examples of mechanical

waves include sound waves, water waves, waves in strings, etc.

Electromagnetic waves do not require a medium to travel through. They

are comprised of vibrating electric and magnetic fields and there are no particle

vibrations at all. This means electromagnetic waves are able to travel through a

vacuum. Examples of electromagnetic waves include light, radio waves, x-rays etc.

The above discussion of wave propagation is depending on whether the waves

require a material medium for their propagation or not. It is also possible to

explain about wave propagation depending on the relation between the direction

of propagation of the wave and the direction of vibrations of the particles of the

medium. On this basis, waves can be classified as transverse and longitudinal

Transverse and Longitudinal Waves

A transverse wave is a wave where the direction of propagation of the wave

is perpendicular to the direction of vibrations of particles of the medium. In

other words, in transverse waves, the directions of the particles' vibrations are at

right angles to the direction of energy transfer (wave movement). Examples of

transverse waves include all electromagnetic waves, waves on strings etc. Figure

### 6.7 shows a transverse wave on the string. To generate such a wave, start by tying

one end of a long string or rope to a wall. Pull on the free end with your hand,

producing a tension in the string, and then move your hand up and down. Note

that the wave travels in the horizontal direction, even though your hand oscillates

vertically about one spot. The displacement of particles in a string is at right

angles to the direction of propagation of the wave.

> **Key Concept:**

In a transverse wave,

the displacement of

individual particles

is at right angles

to the direction of

propagation of the

wave. Figure 6.7 Example of transverse wave on a string.

In longitudinal waves the direction of propagation of the wave (the direction

of energy transfer) is parallel to (in the same direction as) the direction of vibrations of particles of the medium. This means, the vibrations are forward and

backward along the wave. Examples of longitudinal waves include sound waves,

pressure waves, etc. Propagation of longitudinal waves results in the areas of

compressions and rarefactions. Compressions refer to regions where the particles

are pushed together whereas, rarefactions refer to regions where the particles

move apart (see Figure 6.8 ). Compressions and rarefactions can be considered

as the longitudinal version of a crest and a trough, respectively. Moreover, if the

medium of propagation is gas, compressions and rarefactions can be taught of as

regions of high and low pressures, respectively.

### 6.5 Superposition of Waves

At the end of this section, you should be able to:

• define superposition principle;

• explain how standing waves are formed;

• define interference of waves.

When two or more waves pass through a single point at the same time the resultant instantaneous displacement at that point is the sum of the displacements

that would be created separately by each wave, taking signs in to account. This

principle is said to be the superposition principle.

Superposition is also known as Interference. Interference can be either constructive or destructive depending on the phase between the interfering waves.

Two waves are said to be in phase when corresponding points of each wave reach

maximum or minimum displacements at the same time. When two periodic

waves with the same frequency and wavelength travel in the same direction in

phase, their resultant wave is more amplified and we can say that the two waves

interfere constructively.

If two periodic waves with the same frequency and wavelength travel in the

same direction, but out of phase, the resulting wave is diminished (or may be

zero) in amplitude. In such a case the two waves interfere destructively.

> **Key Concept:**

Superposition occurs when two or

more waves pass

through a single

point at the same

time.

Standing Waves

The superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions in the

same medium gives standing (stationary) wave. If you have ever plucked a guitar

string, or blown across the mouth of a pop bottle to create a tone, you have

generated standing waves. In general, a standing wave is one that oscillates with

time, but remains fixed in its location. It is in this sense that the wave is said to be

"standing."

The positions in the medium at which maximum displacement occurs are

called antinodes (A) and those positions with zero displacement are called nodes

(N). Note that:

• The distance between adjacent antinodes is equal to λ

• The distance between adjacent nodes is equal to λ

2 .

sound.

describes your perception of the energy of the sound. The loudness of

a sound is measured in decibel (dB). Timbre is a general term for the

distinguishable characteristics of a tone.

### 📄 Textbook Page 134 — Structured Curriculum Text

134 Unit 6 Mechanical Oscillation and Sound Wave

### 📝 Unit Summary

• Oscillation, also known as periodic motion is a to and fro motion

about a fixed point called equilibrium position.

• Wave is a disturbance that propagates from source carrying energy.

Waves that require material medium for their propagation are called

mechanical waves; and those which do not require medium for their

propagation are known as electromagnetic waves.

• Transverse waves are waves in which their direction of propagation

is perpendicular to the direction of vibrations of the particles of the

medium. However, the direction of movement of some waves is

parallel to the direction of vibrations of particles of the medium.

Such waves are called longitudinal waves.

• Sound waves are the most common example of longitudinal waves.

They travel through any material medium with a speed that depends

on the properties (density) of the medium.

• When two or more waves pass through a single point at the same

time the resultant instantaneous displacement at that point is the

sum of the displacements that would be created separately by each

wave, taking signs in to account. This principle is said to be the

superposition principle. The superposition of two identical waves

travelling in opposite directions in the same medium gives standing

(stationary) wave.

End of Unit Questions and Problems

Part I: Conceptual questions and workout problems

1. Calculate the period of a simple pendulum of length 4m.

2. An object of mass 2kg is attached to one end of a spring of spring

constant 800N/m. If the object is undergoing periodic motion on a

smooth horizontal surface, what is the period of oscillation?

3. Explain the difference in the speed of sound:

(a) between solids, liquids and gases

## 7.1 Temperature and Our Life
*Grade 9 Physics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 139 of 173 (PDF Page 145) • Grade 9 Physics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (7.1 Temperature and Our Life):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 140):** Concept of temperature vs heat, human body temperature regulation, weather, and environmental thermal effects.
> • Curriculum Focus: Concept of temperature vs heat, human body temperature regulation, weather, and environmental thermal effects.
> • Zeroth & First Laws of Thermodynamics: Zeroth Law defines temperature via thermal equilibrium. First Law (Energy Conservation): ΔU = Q - W, where ΔU is change in internal energy, Q is heat added, and W is work done by gas (W = ∫P dV).
> • Four Standard Thermodynamic Processes: 1) Isochoric (constant V, W = 0, ΔU = Q); 2) Isobaric (constant P, W = PΔV); 3) Isothermal (constant T, ΔU = 0, Q = W = nRT ln(V_f/V_i)); 4) Adiabatic (Q = 0, ΔU = -W, PV^γ = constant).
> • Second Law of Thermodynamics: Clausius statement: Heat cannot spontaneously flow from cold to hot without external work. Kelvin-Planck statement: No heat engine can convert all absorbed heat completely into work. Entropy S increases in irreversible isolated processes (ΔS ≥ 0).
> • Heat Engines & Carnot Efficiency: Thermal efficiency η = W / Q_H = 1 - (Q_C / Q_H). Ideal reversible Carnot engine operating between temperatures T_H and T_C has maximum possible efficiency: η_Carnot = 1 - (T_C / T_H), where temperatures MUST be in Kelvin.

---

130o F (54oC ) often leads to heat stroke.

1. Stay well-hydrated to best avoid heat-related illness. Drink enough

heated. If you feel yourself getting too hot, loosen your clothing or

remove excess clothing until you feel cool enough.

3. Wear sunscreen when possible to avoid sunburn, which makes it

> • Concept & Classification of Forces: Force is a push or pull (vector, Newton N = kg·m/s²). Contact forces (normal force, friction, tension) vs Field forces (gravity, electrostatics, magnetism). Friction f = μN resists sliding motion.
> • Newton's Laws of Motion: 1) First Law (Inertia): Body remains at rest or uniform velocity unless acted upon by net external force ΣF ≠ 0; 2) Second Law: ΣF = m·a; 3) Third Law: Action-reaction pairs equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on DIFFERENT objects.
> • Work Done by Constant Force: W = F · d cos θ (Joules J = N·m). Work is scalar. Positive if force assists motion (θ < 90°); Negative if force opposes motion (friction, θ = 180°); Zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).
> • Energy Forms & Conservation: Kinetic Energy KE = 0.5 m v²; Gravitational Potential Energy PE = m g h. Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E_total = KE + PE = constant in isolated system without non-conservative friction losses.

5. Thermistor

A thermistor is a resistance thermometer, or a resistor whose resistance

> 🖼️ **Figure 7.12 Thermistor thermometer.**

> *(Original textbook diagram/illustration — View crisp illustration in the "Exact Page" tab)*

is dependent on temperature. The term is a combination of 'thermal' and

'resistor'. It is made of metallic oxides, pressed into a bead, disk, or cylindrical shape and then encapsulated with an impermeable material such as

glass. There are two types of thermistors: Negative Temperature Coefficient

(NTC) and Positive Temperature Coefficient (PTC). With NTC thermistor,

when the temperature increases, resistance decreases. Conversely, when

temperature decreases, resistance increases. This type of thermistor is used

the most. A PTC thermistor works a little differently. When temperature

increases, the resistance increases, and when temperature decreases, resistance decreases. This type of thermistor is generally used as a fuse. Typically,

a thermistor achieves high precision within a limited temperature range of

about 50oC around the target temperature. This range is dependent on the

base resistance

6. Radiation Thermometers

> 🖼️ **Figure 7.13 A radiation thermometer.**

> *(Original textbook diagram/illustration — View crisp illustration in the "Exact Page" tab)*

Radiation thermometers are not based on any change of property with temperature but use the electromagnetic radiation from a body to be measured.

As the body warms up, the total radiation it emits increases rapidly and

the spectral distribution shifts to shorter wavelengths. The temperature

can thus be determined by measuring the radiation, and there is a clear

advantage that all the detecting equipments is remote from the hot body.

The application areas of radiation thermometer are quite extensive. They

are frequently used in industrial processes, the professional sector and in

particular to monitor main supply units or to measure the temperature of

components in motors or machines. Glass and electrical industries use

many forms of radiation thermometers.

What happens

At the end of this section, you should be able to:

rate;

• calculate temperature dependent linear expansion of materials.

In the previous section you have learnt about temperature, effects of temperature,

different temperature scales, and all temperature related issues. Now we are going

to see the thermal expansion of materials.

Different materials expand or contract at different rates. In general, gases expand

more than liquids, and liquids expand more than solids. Observation of thermal

expansion in a solid object requires careful analysis. Understanding the expansion

of metals is very crucial for using them in different technological applications.

Have you ever found the metal lid on a glass jar too tight to open? One solution

is to run hot water over the lid, to loosen it because the metal expands more

than the glass does. To varying extents, most materials expand when heated and

contract when cooled.

when cooled. The increase in any one dimension of a solid is called linear expansion, linear in the sense that the expansion occurs along a line. Figure 7.16

decreases to L0 − ∆L.

For modest temperature changes, experiments show that the change in length

(∆L) is directly proportional to the change in temperature ∆T .

when cooled. The increase in any one dimension of a solid is called linear expansion, linear in the sense that the expansion occurs along a line. Figure 7.16

illustrates the linear expansion of a rod whose length is L0 at temperature T0.

where ∆T and ∆L are the magnitude of the changes in temperature and length

respectively. Conversely when the temperature decreases to T0 − ∆T , the length

decreases to L0 − ∆L.

For modest temperature changes, experiments show that the change in length

(∆L) is directly proportional to the change in temperature ∆T .

> **Key Concept:**

T Linear expansion: the increase in length of a substance due to heating.

T Coefficient of linear expansion: the increase in length of a 1 m road of

a given substance when its temperature increases by 1 K.

example of linear

expansion occurs

material. We know

that the material

itself expands when

heated. What about

the hole? Does it

expand, contract, or

remain the same?

∆L ∝ ∆T (7.8)

In addition, the change in length is proportional to the initial length of the

rod.

∆L ∝ L0 (7.9)

From the above two equations we conclude that,

∆L ∝ L0∆T (7.10)

economy.

the increase in temperatures around the world due to greenhouse

gases.

called thermometer.

> • Curriculum Focus: Pioneering discoveries by Galileo, Newton, Faraday, Maxwell, Marie Curie, Einstein, and modern physicists.
> • Meaning & Scope of Physics: Physics (from the Greek word "phusis" meaning nature) is the fundamental natural science that investigates matter, energy, space, time, and their reciprocal interactions. Its scope ranges from subatomic quarks (10⁻¹⁸ m) to the cosmic expanse (10²⁶ m).
> • Core Branches of Physics (Table 1.1 in Textbook): 1) Mechanics (motion with or without reference to forces); 2) Thermodynamics (heat, temperature, and energy transformations); 3) Optics (light properties, lenses, and lasers); 4) Electromagnetism (electric charges, currents, and magnetic fields); 5) Acoustics (sound production and wave transmission); 6) Nuclear & Quantum Physics (atomic nuclei, radioactivity, and energy quantization).
> • Interdisciplinary Fields: Biophysics (applying physics laws to biological mechanisms and nerve impulses); Geophysics (seismic waves and tectonic activity in the Ethiopian Rift Valley); Medical Physics (X-rays, ultrasound, MRI, radiotherapy); Astrophysics (celestial dynamics and cosmology).
> • Historical Contributors in the Ethiopian Curriculum: Galileo Galilei (scientific method & kinematics); Sir Isaac Newton (laws of motion and universal gravitation); Michael Faraday (electromagnetic induction); Marie Curie (radioactivity discoveries); Albert Einstein (theory of relativity & photoelectric effect).
> • Physics in Ethiopian National Modernization: Hydroelectric generation at the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD, 5,150 MW), satellite communication via ET-SMART, and regional medical imaging infrastructure.

> • Core Branches of Physics (Table 1.1 in Textbook): 1) Mechanics (motion with or without reference to forces); 2) Thermodynamics (heat, temperature, and energy transformations); 3) Optics (light properties, lenses, and lasers); 4) Electromagnetism (electric charges, currents, and magnetic fields); 5) Acoustics (sound production and wave transmission); 6) Nuclear & Quantum Physics (atomic nuclei, radioactivity, and energy quantization).
> • Interdisciplinary Fields: Biophysics (applying physics laws to biological mechanisms and nerve impulses); Geophysics (seismic waves and tectonic activity in the Ethiopian Rift Valley); Medical Physics (X-rays, ultrasound, MRI, radiotherapy); Astrophysics (celestial dynamics and cosmology).
> • Historical Contributors in the Ethiopian Curriculum: Galileo Galilei (scientific method & kinematics); Sir Isaac Newton (laws of motion and universal gravitation); Michael Faraday (electromagnetic induction); Marie Curie (radioactivity discoveries); Albert Einstein (theory of relativity & photoelectric effect).
> • Physics in Ethiopian National Modernization: Hydroelectric generation at the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD, 5,150 MW), satellite communication via ET-SMART, and regional medical imaging infrastructure.
